extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / American citizens evaluating the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the powers conferred by the proposed U.S. Constitution, presenting standards for judging which powers are necessary, dangerous, or properly limited and explaining why specific federal powers are appropriate. Aimed at guiding public judgment about adoption of the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of transferred powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether any part of the powers transferred to the general government be unnecessary or improper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask if a power is a necessary means of attaining a necessary end; critics who dwell only on inconveniences or possible abuses miss that legitimate powers often have incidental evils. Evaluate whether the asserted power is required to advance the public good before condemning it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate power danger test
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the entire mass of powers vested in the general government is dangerous to the portion of jurisdiction left in the several States?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the aggregate federal authority against the sovereignty and functions retained by the states; examine whether the totality of transferred powers threatens state jurisdiction or is appropriate given national aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step decision rule for conferring power
rubrics_metrics.description: First decide whether such a power is necessary to the public good; if yes, then guard as effectually as possible against perversion of the power to the public detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy for evaluating powers: (1) necessity test, then (2) design protections and limits (e.g., appropriation terms, representation structures) to reduce risks of abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify powers by public objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers should be reviewed by reducing them into classes relating to: (1) security against foreign danger; (2) regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) maintenance of harmony among the States; (4) miscellaneous objects of general utility; (5) restraint of the States from injurious acts; (6) provisions for giving due efficacy to all these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural guidance for analysis: group governmental powers according to their object to form a clear judgment about their necessity and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: National defense powers must be effectually confided
rubrics_metrics.description: Security against foreign danger is a primitive object of civil society and the powers requisite for attaining it must be effectually confided to the federal councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes declaring war, letters of marque, providing armies and fleets, regulating militia, levying and borrowing money. Treat defense powers as essential and justify federal authority to ensure national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to declare war is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of declaring war is necessary and established in ample form by the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No extensive proof required; treat declaration of war as an indispensable sovereign power of the national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite power to raise troops and maintain forces
rubrics_metrics.description: It was necessary to give an indefinite power of raising troops and providing fleets, and of maintaining both in peace as well as in war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: one cannot safely limit defensive force if offense by other nations cannot be limited; preparations in peacetime may be essential to deter or meet unexpected threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutional barriers that encourage usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vain to oppose constitutional barriers to the impulse of self-preservation; rigid prohibitions may produce habitual usurpations in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional rules that allow needed discretion for security while minimizing routine circumvention; over-restrictive rules may create precedents of necessary violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance standing army dangers against necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing force is dangerous though it may be necessary; prudence requires diminishing both the necessity and the danger of resorting to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical examples (Charles VII's military establishments, Rome) to weigh long-term liberty costs; seek constitutional safeguards (e.g., appropriation limits) while retaining necessary defense capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit terms for revenue appropriations supporting armies
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation of the term for which revenue may be appropriated to army support is a clear precaution (Constitution ties appropriation to two years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short appropriation terms (two years) constrain military establishments and align with representation frequency; compare with British practice (parliamentary discretion in practice limited to one year) to argue the safety of the American arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and election frequency justify appropriation discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because representatives are elected freely by the whole body of the people every second year, Congress can be safely entrusted with discretion over appropriations limited to two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional design (frequent, broad-based elections) as a safeguard against misuse of military appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide and maintain a navy
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to provide and maintain a navy is plainly necessary and is among the greatest blessings of America for maritime defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national navy supports security of maritime frontiers; such batteries are less capable of being turned against domestic liberties than standing armies on land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to levy and borrow money is necessary and properly broad
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of levying and borrowing money, being the sinew of national defense, is properly vested in the federal government and necessary in the extent and form given by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject limiting federal taxation to external taxation only; revenues from commerce vary over time and a durable government must be able to adapt to economic evolution (agricultural to manufacturing phases).

rubrics_metrics.name: General-welfare language must be limited by enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'to lay and collect taxes... to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare' does not amount to an unlimited commission to exercise every power alleged necessary for the general welfare; it must be read alongside the subsequent enumeration of particular powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive principle: general clauses are explained and qualified by following specific enumerations; one should not read the general phrase as a blank check to legislate in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform federal authority over foreign intercourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers which regulate intercourse with foreign nations (treaties, ambassadors, piracy, foreign commerce) should be vested in the general government because if the nation is one, it should be one in respect to other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized authority avoids contradictory state-level foreign policies that would undermine national unity externally; includes power to prohibit slave importation after 1808 per clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to make treaties and appoint public ministers/consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors and other public ministers and consuls are proper; inclusion of consuls is expressly necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the term 'ambassador' narrowly; the Constitution improves on Confederation by explicitly authorizing lower-grade ministers and consuls to suit practical needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to define and punish piracy and high-seas felonies
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government must have the power to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations, for certainty and uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because terms like 'felony' vary across state codes and common law, a legislative federal definition is necessary to avoid inconsistent standards and to prevent individual states embroiling the Union with foreign nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate foreign commerce is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of foreign commerce belongs properly to the federal administration and is too important to be left incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal commerce power prevents states from nullifying national commercial policy and ensures effective national negotiation and enforcement of commercial treaties and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prohibit slave importation (deferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution postpones prohibition of slave importation until 1808; this limitation should be viewed as a substantial point gained in favor of humanity, not as criminal toleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the clause as a compromise that allows ultimate abolition by the federal government and discourages the traffic in the interim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal regulation of interstate commerce prevents internal duties and animosities
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal power to regulate commerce among the several States (and with Indian tribes) is necessary to prevent states from imposing tolls/duties on goods passing through their jurisdictions and to avoid reciprocal grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and foreign examples (Switzerland, Germany, Netherlands) show that lack of an overarching authority produces tolls and customs that harm national commerce and peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear authority over trade with Indian tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of commerce with Indian tribes must be unfettered by the confusing limitations found in the Articles of Confederation to avoid contradictions about which Indians are 'members' of a State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguities in prior arrangements produced perplexity and conflict; explicit federal authority avoids intrusion on state rights while ensuring uniformity where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to coin money and regulate value of foreign coin
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal power to coin money and regulate the value thereof, and of foreign coin, is necessary to preserve uniform currency value across the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If foreign coin value were left to states, uniformity of value would be destroyed; a national standard ensures commercial certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to punish counterfeiting of public securities and coin
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment of counterfeiting public securities, as well as current coin, should be vested in the federal government to secure the value of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized authority for counterfeiting prevention preserves financial integrity across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to fix weights and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of weights and measures is a necessary federal power for uniformity in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform standards avoid confusion and fraud in interstate trade akin to the necessity for regulating coin value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform rule of naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The general government should establish a uniform rule of naturalization to avoid the embarrassments and interstate conflicts arising from divergent state naturalization laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divergent state rules could allow an alien proscribed in one state to become a citizen in another and assert rights; uniform national rules prevent such conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform laws of bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing uniform laws of bankruptcy is expedient and connected with commerce to prevent fraud where parties or property move between states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national bankruptcy law reduces opportunities for forum-shopping and fraudulent behavior across state lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform rule for proof and effect of public acts and records
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should prescribe by general laws the manner in which public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and their effect in other States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides convenience and justice, especially on state borders where processes or records may be transferred or become operative across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish post offices and post roads
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to establish post offices and post roads is harmless and useful to facilitate intercourse between the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging communication and transit is a legitimate federal function that promotes commerce and unity without infringing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence: choose the greater, not the perfect, good
rubrics_metrics.description: In political institutions the choice must be of the lesser evil or the greater, not the perfect, good—accept imperfections if the institution advances public happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that all institutions have alloy; practical judgments should weigh trade-offs between benefits and possible abuses rather than demand perfection.
